question: Does each change to the training data give the policy its own skill, and only that skill? And can a probe that changes the world mid-episode tell whether the skill is there?
measure: Follow gain: how far the jaws (or the set-down cube) move when the cube or the square is moved 20 mm mid-episode, as a fraction of the move (0 = ignored, 1 = followed). Pickups kept: pickups with the probe over pickups in the same episodes left alone. Each probed episode is paired with its untouched twin on 100 placements. 55 predictions were written down before the run.
outcome: Mixed. The two data changes we aimed give their skills: trained on a self-correcting teacher, policies follow a moved cube (+0.73 against +0.04 for ACT); trained on random servos, they keep pickups when the elbow goes soft (62 of 73 against 35 of 87). But of all 55 predictions, 32 held and 23 failed. 19 of the failures are one probe: every policy, baselines included, sets the cube down on a square that moved (+0.51 to +0.96 on the nominal scene, scripted teacher 0.00), although no data change aimed at that.
setup: A policy is the network that drives the arm. We have two kinds: ACT (a transformer) and a small CNN. Both read a wrist-camera frame and output a chunk of the next 90 joint commands. Execute 90 runs the whole chunk; execute 30 replans every 30 commands. The teacher is the scripted controller in the simulator that knows the true cube position; policies learn by imitating it. The recipe we want to test says: a policy trained by imitation learns only the skills its data forces. That is three claims. (1) A data change produces the skill. (2) A probe detects it. (3) The skill is what buys success. A success count cannot test them, because a policy that keeps looking and one that only remembers the first frame both succeed when nothing changes. A probe changes the world mid-episode and compares with the same episode left alone. The pair is meant to differ only by the change. We probed checkpoints we already had. Baseline: no data change. Perturbed teacher ("look"): the teacher starts off-target and recentres, so the data contains corrections. Physics v2 ("motor"): each servo's strength is random, soft to stiff. The probes: shift_placement moves cube and square 20 mm at action 100, after the survey frame at action 90. swap_elbow turns the elbow servo into the other kind (soft or stiff) at action 100. drop_cube puts the cube back once it is lifted. move_square moves the square once the cube is lifted. Scenes: nominal (stiff elbow), servo (the measured soft elbow), high-lift (servo scene, 100 mm lift). "matrix" below means the report file matrix.json; "recomputed" means made on Nov 25 from the stored per-episode rows and traces with the repository's own scoring functions, with no new simulation.

parts.title: Is the probe itself sound?
parts.why: If the probe reads a skill where there is none, no policy result means anything.
parts.did: Ran two reference controls on all three scenes. The plain teacher is open-loop (it never looks again), so its follow gain must be 0. The same teacher told about the change in advance must read 1 and still succeed.

parts.title: "Look": does training on corrections make a policy follow a cube that moved?
parts.why: This tests claim 1 for the perturbed teacher. If a baseline policy followed the cube too, the skill would need no data change.
parts.did: Moved cube and square 20 mm at action 100 on the nominal SO-101 scene. CNN numbers are pooled over 3 seeds.

predictions.text: Baseline ACT, execute 90: absent or partial
Perturbed-teacher ACT, execute 30: partial or present
Baseline ACT, execute 30: partial or present (it reads four frames before closing)

parts.conclusion: The data change produces the skill: +0.55 and +0.73 with corrections in the data, +0.01 and +0.04 without. Replanning alone does not: the baseline ACT at execute 30 looks at four frames and still ignores the shift (+0.06). That was the one failed prediction here. Not predicted: the physics v2 ACT at execute 30 follows the shift (+0.87) with no data aimed at that. The full matrix shows the same for the high-lift ACT (+0.61) and the fair CNN (+0.64) at execute 30, so the servo data brings some of this skill with it. The perturbed ACT at execute 30 picks up only 7 of 100 unprobed, so "9 of 7" is not a usable ratio.

parts.title: "Motor": does training on random servos make a policy keep its grip when the elbow goes soft?
parts.why: This tests claim 1 for physics v2, and checks that each skill comes from its own data change and not from the other one.
parts.did: Swapped the elbow servo to the measured soft one at action 100 on the nominal scene and counted pickups against the untouched episodes.

predictions.text: Baseline ACT, execute 90 and execute 30: absent
Physics v2 CNN and ACT (execute 90 and 30): present

parts.conclusion: Physics v2 policies keep their pickups; baseline policies lose most of them. The perturbed-teacher policies, which have the "look" skill, do no better here than the baselines (41 of 246 and 26 of 77). So "look" does not bring "motor" with it. This probe measures coping with a changed servo, not identifying it.

parts.title: Is the skill what buys success?
parts.why: Claim 3. A policy could follow the cube and still fail to pick it up, or keep picking up without following.
parts.did: Across the learned-policy cells under shift_placement, compared follow gain with pickups kept (matrix, 32 cells; one cell with no pickups unprobed is left out).

parts.conclusion: Following and kept pickups rise together across cells. The thresholds fail as registered: the three perturbed CNN seeds follow (+0.60, +0.54, +0.51) and keep under 70%, and 7 low-gain cells keep 32% to 50%. The correlation is a ranking over cells that share checkpoints, seeds and placements, and that also differ in network and replanning rate. It does not show that following keeps a given pickup. Recomputed per episode: among the perturbed CNN's episodes with gain 0.5 or more, 28 of 50, 22 of 43 and 22 of 41 keep the pickup, because half of 20 mm still leaves up to 10 mm.

The full record is 32 held and 23 failed. 19 of the 23 are move_square: 18 groups follow the square, and one (baseline ACT at execute 30 on the servo scene) picks up 0 of 100 unprobed, has nothing to compare, and is counted failed by the report although it is unreadable. parts.title: Do policies really follow a moved square, or does the probe invent it?
parts.why: The note said in advance that a policy following a moved square counts against "data alone decides". Before accepting that, rule out a number produced without the policy doing anything.
parts.did: Read the scoring code and the per-episode traces. The square moves 20 mm once the cube is 15 mm up; only the square moves. The gain is the cube's final position against the untouched twin, along the move.

predictions.text: move_square, every policy on every scene: absent (no data change targets it). 19 predictions.

head: Policy group
Nominal: gain
Nominal: cube ends on moved square
Servo: gain

parts.conclusion: It is real. The gain is a paired difference, so where the untouched cube lands cancels. Both cubes end at rest (height differs by 1.0 mm at most). Sideways drift averages -0.04 to +0.06 of the move. The jaws do not move until the next camera frame is read, then move +0.47 to +0.91 of the way. The open-loop teacher reads 0. Proven: the policies carry the cube to the moved square. Only suggested: why. All policies were trained on random placements with the square in view during the carry, so ordinary data may already force it; no file tests that.

parts.title: Does any policy retry after a dropped cube?
parts.why: A retry would be a second skill nobody trained. Three nominal-scene groups read "partial" in the recomputed rows.
parts.did: The probe puts the cube back at its start once it has risen 15 mm, and counts a regrasp when the cube is 10 mm up again from 10 actions later. Read the height and gripper traces of every counted episode.

predictions.text: drop_cube, every policy on every scene: absent (no training episode contains a failed grasp). 19 predictions: 16 held, 3 read partial.

cells: every group on the servo and high-lift scenes

parts.conclusion: No policy retries. In the 42 counted episodes the jaws never reopen, and in 41 the cube is already 10 mm up at the first action the count looks at. Closed jaws took the cube along again. The three "partial" verdicts are the probe's counting rule, not a skill. Why it happens only on the nominal scene was not determined.

trust.text: Predictions and verdict thresholds were written to a file and committed (4306f26) before any learned policy was probed.
Each probed episode is paired with the same episode left alone, on 100 teacher-screened placements not used elsewhere. Every policy on a scene gets the same shift.
The reference controls read 0 and 1 on all three scenes, for the shift probe and for the square-move probe.
Where matrix.json has a number, the Nov 25 recomputation from stored rows and traces matches it exactly.

18 of the 55 verdicts counted here (drop_cube and move_square for the 9 nominal-scene groups) are recomputed and are not in matrix.json yet. The nominal-scene result files lost three probes when experiment 53 re-ran those cells with a shorter probe list.

A learned policy's two paired episodes are not identical before the change: commands differ by a median of 0 but up to 0.10 command units in the worst episode, jaws by up to 8.6 mm in the worst pair. The teacher's pairs are identical. The cause was not looked for. It has no direction and the mean jaw displacement is 0.00 until the next frame is read.
Why the policies follow a moved square is not established. Every checkpoint was trained on random placements, so there is no policy without that to compare.
The drop_cube count takes a cube carried up again by closed jaws for a regrasp. Its three "partial" verdicts are not retries.
One cell (baseline ACT, execute 30, servo scene) picks up 0 of 100 unprobed. Its move_square verdict is n/a and its drop_cube verdict rests on 1 drop.

The controls job first exited with an error (the teacher has no solution for some placements on the high-lift scene). Fixed on Nov 21 (commit 099f3c9): such placements are left out and the zero control is read on the median.
ACT has one seed per kind. Checkpoints came from different earlier experiments, so the kinds also differ in data size and scene. Simulation only.
The per-episode readings (jaw timing, millimetres left, gripper traces) are analyses made after the run, not registered tests.

meaning: The recipe held where it was aimed: one data change, its skill, detected by a probe whose controls pass. That part is enough for experiment 53, whose own numbers use the same two probes and stand. The other half did not hold. The recipe also said no skill appears without a data change aimed at it, and named a policy following a moved square as evidence against. Every learned policy does that, baselines included. And the servo data brings some following of a moved cube at execute 30. So "data decides which skills exist" may still be true, but we cannot predict the skills from the changes we made on purpose: the ordinary data (random placements, the square in view) seems to teach some already. Experiment 53 needs two caveats: its opening line "one data change gives one feature" is true only for the aimed pair, and the skill it names as a harder next rung (set-down on a moved square) is already there. The link between following and kept pickups is a ranking, not the registered 70% and 30% levels.
lesson: Write the predictions down first, and then read all of them. A prediction that fails in all 18 groups where it can be read is not noise. It sat unread because the report printed "not run" for half of it and the headline had already been told. When a tool re-runs part of a result, check that it did not drop what was there.
